---
title: "Measuring Dependence"
---

How do we put a *number* on the statement "these two variables move together"?
This chapter climbs a ladder from the most familiar measure to the most
general, and at the top we look back and see that every rung was one of just
**two roads**.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Spine — Two Roads

There are really only two ways to ask "how much do these move together?"

1. **Without the distribution** — compare the data directly via a *transform*
   and a *distance*.  One template covers Pearson, Spearman, distance
   correlation, and kernels:

   ```
   measure = compare( transform(x) , transform(y) )
   ```

2. **Through the distribution** — read the dependence out of $p(x,y)$ as
   *information*.  This needs a density, which forces a choice: *assume* its
   shape (parametric, fast, wrong in tails) or *learn* it (generative —
   Gaussianization, flows).

The *transform* is the thread running through both: a hand-picked map on the
first road; a learned, invertible map on the generative branch of the second.
:::

## Why This Matters for Finance

A correlation matrix is the beating heart of portfolio risk — but it only sees
**straight lines**.  Tail co-movements, regime switches, and non-linear
contagion are exactly the dependence that Pearson misses and that mutual
information and kernel measures are built to catch.

The motivating failure: a book your risk report called *diversified* — low
correlations everywhere — falls all at once when one shock arrives.  **What did
the number miss?**  That question drives the whole chapter.

## The Ladder

| Rung | Measure | Road | Sees |
|------|---------|------|------|
| 1 | Pearson $r$ | no density | linear only |
| 2 | Spearman $\rho$ | no density | monotonic |
| 3 | Distance correlation | no density | any dependence |
| 4 | HSIC / CKA | no density | any (kernel test) |
| 5 | Entropy | via density | one variable's budget |
| 6 | Mutual information | via density | any dependence, in **bits** |
| 7 | Linfoot R | via density | any (on $[0,1]$ scale) |
| 8 | Gaussianization | via learned density | all of the above + generation |

## Pages in This Chapter

1. **[Correlation: Pearson and Spearman](01-correlation.qmd)** — the
   comfortable defaults and their blind spots.  Includes the *running
   characters* (two banks; a convex payoff) and the independence reference.
2. **[Kernel Measures: HSIC & CKA](02-kernels-hsic.qmd)** — Road 1 completed:
   independence without a density, why CKA is the readable form of HSIC, and
   how the kernel/bandwidth choice works.
3. **[Mutual Information](03-mutual-information.qmd)** — surprise, entropy, the
   honest measure, and Linfoot's bridge back to the correlation scale.
4. **[From Points to Time Series](04-windows-and-blocks.qmd)** — the window
   dial: scalars → vectors → blocks, with total correlation and block MI
   computed on the real basket.
5. **[Gaussianization](05-gaussianization.qmd)** — learn the density, then
   measure; the two-roads synthesis and the final scorecard.
6. **[Causality](06-causality.qmd)** — correlation ≠ causation; directed
   information and Granger causality.

The hands-on [labs](labs/index.qmd) build each rung in isolation, benchmark
them all together in the **measure zoo**, then hunt the **hidden risk** in a
book the correlation matrix called *diversified*.
